newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea ends huge manhunt for Northern agent.
newsitem.headline: South Korea ends huge manhunt for Northern agent.

text.p: South Korean on Thursday called off a massive manhunt for the last North Korean agent still missing after a submarine landed a group of 26 North Koreans in September, a military spokesman said.
"All troops mobilised to weed out armed infiltrators have returned to their units," the spokesman said. He said routine military checks would continue near the North Korean border.

The manhunt involved about 40,000 South Korean troops at its height and Thursday's decision marks the end of a huge search operation that began on September 17 when the North Korean submarine ran aground off the eastern city of Kangnung.
The spokesman said security forces would remain alert against possible provocations by the North.
Two days earlier, South Korean troops killed two of the last three North Koreans who had escaped capture.
"The one missing might have died already. Continuing a huge operation to look for him is believed to be ineffective managment of troops," said a senior officer, who declined to be named.
Seoul officials have said of the original 26 North Korean infiltrators, 13 were shot dead, one captured and eleven others killed themselves.
The Shark-class submarine ran aground off Kangnung as it tried to pick up three North Korean spies it had offloaded two days earlier, according to Lee Kwang-soo, the only North Korean captured alive.
Lee has confirmed that all the spies were killed and the man still at large was a submarine crew member.
President Kim Young-sam on Thursday repeated that strengthening national security would remain one of his priorities.

"We live in a situation where we don't know when and how North Korea will stage a provocation. We should be fully prepared to cope with any situation," Kim's spokesman quoted him as saying in a meeting with advisers.
South Korean Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung said the North had not given up its policy of taking the South by force.
Lee was speaking at the funeral on Thursday of three South Korean soldiers who were killed during a fierce gun battle with two fleeing Northern agents on Tuesday.
Tension has remained high on the peninsula, the world's last Cold War frontier, since the stranded submarine was spotted by a taxi driver in Kangnung.

Seoul has demanded an apology from North Korea over the incident while Pyongyang has threatened to retaliate "a hundredfold or a thousandfold" for the deaths of its agents and called for the return of their bodies, any survivors, and the submarine.
